title: ABCD SYNDROME
alt_titles: ALBINISM, BLACK LOCK, CELL MIGRATION DISORDER OF THE NEUROCYTES OF THE GUT, AND DEAFNESS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene (131244) on chromosome 13q22.

paragraphs.text: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive neural crest syndrome. Its name comes from its features: albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease), and deafness (Gross et al., 1995; Verheij et al., 2002). Verheij et al. (2002) noted that the phenotype clearly overlaps with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome, which comprises sensorineural deafness, hypopigmentation of the skin, hair and irides, and Hirschsprung disease.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) reported a macrosomic newborn girl born to consanguineous Kurdish parents. She had albinism, a black lock of hair at the right temporo-occipital region, retinal depigmentation, and bilateral deafness confirmed by brainstem auditory-evoked potentials. She also had a severe defect of intestinal innervation. Biopsy showed aganglionosis of the large intestine and a total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine, indicating a total lack of sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. She died of intestinal dysfunction at 5 weeks of age. She was the 14th child of her parents. Four of her sibs had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth, and the other 9 sibs were well. Gross et al. (1995) considered this combination of albinism, black lock, deafness, and total lack of intestinal neural innervation to be a previously unreported neural crest syndrome and named it ABCD syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) concluded that ABCD syndrome shows autosomal recessive inheritance. Their reasoning was that 5 children of consanguineous Kurdish parents were affected while 9 of their sibs were well. Verheij et al. (2002) supported recessive inheritance when they found a homozygous EDNRB mutation in the index patient of this family.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) concluded that ABCD syndrome shows autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) based the autosomal recessive inheritance conclusion for ABCD syndrome on 5 affected children of consanguineous Kurdish parents, while 9 of their sibs were well.
checks.evidence_quote: She was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents. Four sibs of our patient had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth. The other 9 sibs are well
checks.explanation: The proband plus 4 affected sibs gives 5 affected children, with 9 well sibs, from consanguineous parents.

paragraphs.text: Verheij et al. (2002) found a homozygous EDNRB mutation in ABCD syndrome, and the phenotype overlaps with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome. For these reasons they suggested that ABCD syndrome is an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome rather than a separate entity.
